clue.text: Strip cut short before boy looked

indicators.note: cut short means the word for the strip loses its final letter

parts.note: the Gaza Strip, the territory on the eastern Mediterranean
Ed is a common boy's name, short for Edward

explanation.surface: A garment shortened, and then a lad stared at it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strip' looks like clothing or undressing, but it is the Gaza Strip; 'cut short' trims GAZA to GAZ.
explanation.definitionFit: To gaze is to look steadily, so the past tense is a straight synonym of looked.

clue.text: Cheap stretcher bearing up fighter, cold

indicators.note: up, in a down clue, means the fighter's name is read from bottom to top

parts.note: the MiG is a Russian fighter jet
a rack was a device for stretching a victim

explanation.surface: A shoddy stretcher carries an injured, chilled soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stretcher' looks like a medical carrier but is the torture rack; 'up' turns MIG into GIM.
explanation.definitionFit: A gimcrack thing is showy but flimsy and worthless, so cheap in quality.

clue.text: Being irrational, a number's stored in variables

indicators.note: stored in means the pieces are kept inside the other letters

parts.note: z is a standard algebraic variable, so variables are Zs
nine is a number, and nine's (nine is) gives the letters with S

explanation.surface: A digit has been saved inside the changing values of a program.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variables' are algebraic unknowns, here two Zs, and 'stored in' puts A NINES between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Zaniness is crazy, absurd behaviour, a state of being irrational.

clue.text: Kind witch toting pieces in panto

indicators.note: in pieces means the letters are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: A good-natured witch carries props in a Christmas show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pieces' signals rearranging KINDWITCHTOTING. A panto is a British Christmas pantomime, a comic family stage show.
explanation.definitionFit: Dick Whittington is one of the classic British pantomimes, about a boy, his cat and London.

clue.text: Fifteen pounds needs to go on a new driver

indicators.note: to go on means the following pieces are placed after the earlier ones

parts.note: L is the learner plate shown by a new driver in Britain
lb is the abbreviation for pounds in weight
needs means lacks, is without

explanation.surface: A large sum of money is required to buy a car for a learner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fifteen' looks like a number but names a rugby union side, which fields fifteen players; 'to go on' sets the later pieces after the earlier ones.
explanation.definitionFit: The All Blacks are New Zealand's national rugby union team, a side of fifteen players.

clue.text: Seemingly unlikely!

definitions.meaning: seemingly here means in a way that appears to be so
an exclamation of scornful disbelief, as in 'that will never happen'

explanation.walkthrough: The two-word phrase means 'as though' and is also a sarcastic retort.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means 'as though' and, alone, is a scornful exclamation that something will not happen.

clue.text: It was a wonder rogue could contain leaderless army at El Alamein

indicators.note: contain means the word for rogue holds the other piece inside

parts.note: a louse is a contemptible person, a rogue

indicators.note: leaderless means the army's name loses its first letter

parts.note: the British Eighth Army fought the battle of El Alamein in 1942

explanation.surface: A scoundrel managed to hold back a headless force in the desert war.
explanation.walkthrough: The Pharos lighthouse at Alexandria was one of the Seven Wonders. 'leaderless' drops the first letter of the army's name and 'contain' puts what is left inside the rogue.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pharos lighthouse of Alexandria was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

clue.text: Appearance during heat involves support play

indicators.note: involves means the word for support is taken inside the other pieces

parts.note: a look is an appearance
in means during, as in in the night
heat is passion, anger
to back is to support

explanation.surface: A look in the hottest moment brings in a helper.
explanation.walkthrough: The play is John Osborne's 1956 drama; 'involves' puts the support between the appearance and 'during heat'.
explanation.definitionFit: Look Back in Anger is John Osborne's 1956 play, a landmark of British drama.

clue.text: Too much leg displayed under cape's fabric

indicators.note: under, in a down clue, means the other pieces sit below the letter for cape

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cape on maps
OTT, over the top, means too much
on is the leg side in cricket

explanation.surface: Showing too much leg beneath a cloak's material.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leg' is the cricket term: the leg side of the field is also the on side.
explanation.definitionFit: Cotton is a fabric woven from the fibres of the cotton plant.

clue.text: Hospital to run: founder holds that contract

indicators.note: holds means the word for founder keeps the other pieces inside it

parts.note: to founder is to sink
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A hospital is to be run while its founder holds that agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'founder' looks like a noun but is the verb, to sink; 'contract' is a verb too.
explanation.definitionFit: To shrink is to contract, become smaller.

clue.text: Using handcuffs and a stick on person

indicators.note: on means the following pieces come after the word for person

parts.note: a man is a person
to cling is to stick fast

explanation.surface: A police officer restrains someone and wields a truncheon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stick' looks like a weapon, but it is the verb meaning adhere; 'on' sets it and A after the person.
explanation.definitionFit: To manacle is to put handcuffs or shackles on someone, so the participle means using handcuffs.

clue.text: Having smashed into fence, start to throw underarm

indicators.note: smashed into means one piece breaks its way inside the other

parts.note: an oxer is a fence in showjumping or hunting, a hedge with a rail

indicators.note: start to means only the first letter of the following word is used

explanation.surface: A rider crashes through a fence and is then told to bowl underarm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smashed into' puts T, the start of 'throw', inside OXER. OXTER is a Scottish and northern English word for the armpit.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxter is a dialect noun for the armpit, the hollow under the arm.

clue.text: Makes whole series of points after resistance

indicators.note: after means the compass points come after the letter for resistance

parts.note: R is the symbol for electrical resistance
a string of compass points: east, north, east, west, south

explanation.surface: Someone restores things after scoring a run of points despite opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'series of points' is a run of compass-point letters, E, N, E, W, S; 'after' places them behind R.
explanation.definitionFit: To renew something is to restore it, making it whole or fresh again.

clue.text: Inflexible, rejecting objections not made?

indicators.note: rejecting means the word for objections is turned back to front

parts.note: buts are objections, as in no ifs or buts
the saying is that some people are born, not made, so the opposite of made is born

explanation.surface: An unbending person dismisses complaints that were never raised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejecting' turns BUTS into STUB. 'not made?' leans on the saying 'born, not made', the question mark flagging the oblique sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A stubborn person refuses to give way, which is being inflexible in attitude.

clue.text: Female finally took Jack for attention-seeker

indicators.note: finally means only the last letter of the word female is used

parts.note: got means took, obtained
Jack the Ripper, the Victorian murderer

explanation.surface: A woman took a man's name to get noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' looks like any man, but here it is Jack the Ripper.
explanation.definitionFit: An ego tripper indulges in self-centred behaviour, seeking attention and admiration.

clue.text: The sack for those who'd take part

definitions.text: The sack for those who'd take part

parts.words: The sack for those who'd take part
parts.note: sack is slang for bed, and taking a part is landing an acting role, so this is the bed where roles are traded for favours

explanation.surface: Dismissal awaits anyone who joins in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The sack' reads as dismissal, but it is bed; 'take part' is acting, getting a part in a show.
explanation.definitionFit: The casting couch is the notorious idea of a director's couch where acting roles are exchanged for sex.

clue.text: Find different plugs to heat power station

indicators.note: plugs means the rearranged letters fill a gap in the word for heat

parts.note: to warm is to heat

indicators.note: different means the letters are made into a new order

explanation.surface: Look for other plugs to make a generating plant hot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plugs' looks like electrical fittings, but it is the verb: 'different' scrambles 'Find' to INDF, which fills the gap in the word for heat.
explanation.definitionFit: A wind farm is a group of turbines generating electricity, a kind of power station.

clue.text: Short sentence saying whether penned by Chekhov

indicators.note: penned by means the piece is enclosed in the writer's first name

parts.note: Anton Chekhov, the Russian writer

indicators.note: saying means the word for whether is spelt by its sound

parts.note: if can mean whether, as in ask if

explanation.surface: A brief line asks whether something was written by a Russian playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'penned by' encloses the piece in the writer's first name; 'saying' spells the word for whether by sound, IPH.
explanation.definitionFit: An antiphon is a short sentence sung or said before or after a psalm in church.

clue.text: Figures expert can't run with it as it is

indicators.note: run, as stitches or colours run, means the letters are loosened and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone good with numbers won't follow along with things just as they are.
explanation.walkthrough: 'run' looks like a verb about operating, but it signals rearranging CANT and ITASITIS.
explanation.definitionFit: A statistician is a specialist in figures, analysing numerical data.

clue.text: Guile in health club in place of austerity

indicators.note: in means the word for guile sits inside the word for the club

parts.note: a spa is a health club
art is cunning, guile

explanation.surface: Trickery goes on at a fitness centre in a spartan location.
explanation.walkthrough: 'place of austerity' is the Greek city-state, which gave English the word spartan; 'in' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient Sparta was famed for its harsh, austere way of life.

clue.text: Viewer's laughing head off

indicators.note: head off means the first letter is removed

parts.note: jocular means humorous, laughing

explanation.surface: A television watcher's chuckle cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Viewer' is the eye, so 'Viewer's' means of the eye; 'head off' drops J from JOCULAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Ocular means relating to the eye, the organ with which one views.

clue.text: Meals out said to involve mass assortment of sweets

indicators.note: to involve means a letter is taken inside the spoken form
said means the words for meals out are spoken and spelt by sound

parts.note: picnics are meals eaten outdoors
m is the symbol for mass in physics

explanation.surface: Eating out is said to need a lot of a mixed bag of confectionery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said' turns PICNICS into its sound, PICKNIX, and 'to involve' puts M inside. Pick 'n' mix is a British self-service selection of loose sweets.
explanation.definitionFit: Pick 'n' mix is a selection of loose sweets that customers choose themselves, an assortment.

clue.text: Butcher's dismissing queen, greeting statesman

indicators.note: dismissing means the queen's letters are sent away from the word for a look

parts.note: a butcher's is rhyming slang for a look (butcher's hook = look), and a gander is also a look
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword queen
hi is a greeting

explanation.surface: A meat seller sends away royalty and welcomes a politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butcher's' is not a shop: in Cockney rhyming slang 'have a butcher's' means take a look, which is a GANDER; 'dismissing' removes ER.
explanation.definitionFit: Mahatma Gandhi led India's independence movement and is remembered as a statesman.

clue.text: Policeman left in self-contained unit

indicators.note: in means the letter for left goes inside the word for the unit

parts.note: a pod is a self-contained unit, as on a spacecraft

explanation.surface: An officer is left in a detached module.
explanation.walkthrough: Plod is British slang for a police officer, from Mr Plod in the Noddy books.
explanation.definitionFit: Plod is British informal slang for a police officer, from Mr Plod in children's stories.

clue.text: Unbend, dropping ban finally, and have another tenant

indicators.note: dropping means a letter is let fall from the word for unbend

parts.note: to relent is to unbend, soften one's attitude

indicators.note: finally means only the last letter of the following word is used

explanation.surface: A landlord eases up, lifts a prohibition and takes in a new lodger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping' removes N, the last letter of 'ban', from RELENT.
explanation.definitionFit: To relet a property is to let it again, so it gets another tenant.

clue.text: Shower of pork pies and hot fizzy drink keeping short Devon team's return

indicators.note: keeping means the drink holds the other piece inside it

parts.note: pop is a fizzy soft drink

indicators.note: return means the team name is read backwards
short means the team name loses its final letter

parts.note: Plymouth Argyle is the football club from Devon, known as Argyle
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A heap of pastries and a fizzy drink are kept for a football side's homecoming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shower' is one who shows; pork pies is rhyming slang for lies. 'short' and 'return' turn the team's name into LYGRA, which 'keeping' places in the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A polygraph, or lie detector, reveals falsehoods, so it shows up lies.

clue.text: Switch on radar, so locating plant

indicators.note: switch means the letters change places with each other

explanation.surface: Turn the radar on to find a factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant' could mean a factory, but here it is a flower. 'Switch' rearranges ONRADARSO.
explanation.definitionFit: Aaron's rod is a name for great mullein and other tall flowering plants.

clue.text: Type committing a name to memory

parts.note: ROM is read-only memory in computing

explanation.surface: Someone learns a name by heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'committing to' sets A and N after ROM, the memory.
explanation.definitionFit: Roman is the upright style of printing type, as opposed to italic.
